meaning:
When Future says, “Molly keep a nigga motivated, Percocet keep ‘em motivated, good drank keep a nigga motivated,” he’s describing how different drugs affect his motivation or mood:


“Molly” refers to MDMA, a synthetic drug that alters mood and perception. It’s known for producing feelings of euphoria, energy, and increased empathy, which can be interpreted as a source of motivation for him.
“Percocet” is a prescription pain medication containing oxycodone and acetaminophen. It can induce feelings of relaxation and euphoria, possibly providing motivation in a similar way to Molly.
“Good drank” typically refers to a mixture of prescription cough syrup containing codeine and promethazine mixed with a soft drink, like Sprite, creating a concoction known as “lean” or “purple drank.” This mixture can induce feelings of relaxation and euphoria, similar to Percocet.



Overall, Future is suggesting that these drugs help him stay motivated, likely by altering his mood or perception in a way that he finds beneficial.

https://youtu.be/aQDhDnUYn_E?t=24



About this scene:

As revealed years later by Gillian Anderson and confirmed by the filming team, this specific incident was actually not scripted and occurred during filming.

The moment was kept in the final cut because of its authenticity, with Anderson later noting, “And it adds tension to the scene, right?”

In an unusual coincidence, a second unscripted accident happened immediately afterward when a man collided with her as she entered the store. Anderson later reflected on continuing the take, saying, “But I just went on with it.”

During the late 1800’s there was a buzz (no pun intended) surrounding electricity with the usage of arc lightning which is a street light taking off. It took super high amounts of volts to use and because of that, the volts were striking men down and seemingly killing them instantly.

A coroner by the name of Dr. Joseph Fowler who was working on the autopsy at the time was telling the story to his friends at a Buffalo science group. One of the people listening were Alfred P. Southwick, who was a dentist at the time, got the idea of using electricity as a method of electricution.

Diamonds come in many different colors—not just the white “colorless” diamonds we see in Kay commercials. Colorful diamonds are typically produced when trace elements enter and alter the chemical composition of the diamond. The yellow in yellow diamonds, for example, is created by trace amounts of nitrogen.

However, it is still unknown how pink diamonds take on their pinkish hue. Scientists speculate that pink diamonds are created under extreme physical conditions that distort the internal structure of the diamond itself, thus, refracting the light in a different manner and producing the pinkish tint.

These conditions are very rare, and it is estimated that 90% of the world’s pink diamonds come from the Argyle Mine in Australia, which is scheduled to shut down in 2020. As such, natural pink diamonds, are some of the most rare, expensive and, therefore, desirable diamonds in the world.

Days before this album was released, a story went public saying that Future was releasing back-to-back LPs because he lost a lawsuit to Rocko. It stated: “Future had to give him 50% of the money he’s going to make on tour and all of his album royalties.” This made fans mad because it seemed like Future was just rushing out product to pay off Rocko. When asked about it, Future said, “Shit gon’ get took care of. When niggas go broke they do dumb shit. Don’t know what’s going on. We making hits, we making history. Nigga wanna be a part of history you gotta do something to tag along—tag along niggas.”

Drake knows all about these types of fallacies. On his “9,” he says, “If they don’t have a story these days, they’ll make one.”

Insanity is a defense to a crime that may result in the accused being acquitted.  An insanity plea is based on the argument that although the accused may have committed the act prohibited by law, the accused did so without the mental state required to be found guilty.

An insanity plea may result in a “not guilty” verdict, but the accused may be committed to a mental institution.  The most successful insanity pleas are those that result in the accused’s complete freedom.

A famous example of a case involving a successful insanity plea is that of Lorena Bobbitt (pictured below), who in 1994 was acquitted of the crime of chopping off her husband’s penis.  A jury acquitted her after finding that she was temporarily insane.  She was freed after spending only five weeks in a mental hospital.

line: Cain and Abel, both brains, one man, too impeccable
vault_lines: Cain and Abel, both brains, one man, too impeccable
meaning:
The interpretation of this line relies heavily on one somewhat indistinguishable word. Future either says

“Cain and Abel, both brave,”
or “both brains”

The meaning of this lyric comes from Genesis chapter four and the story of Adam’s two sons, Cain and Abel.

The story details how each brother made his own offerings to God. Abel tended animals and Cain the soil, but God favors the offering of Abel as he seemingly gives God a more suitable testament:

“fat portions from some of the firstborn of his flock.” (Genesis 4:4)

Cain, in fury, kills his younger brother Abel and is then cursed by God.



Giovanni Domenico Ferretti, Cain and Abel, 1740

Many interpret this story as a reminder to give God your best, prioritize God, however, in one line, Future challenges this assumption. He either condones the actions of Cain, with “both brave” or implies that he himself, “one man,” has both sides of the two original brothers, “both brains.” There is a clear division between the brothers in Christian interpretation as good and evil, right and sin, so using the “both brains” interpretation, Future may imply he has both the sin and the good making him “too impeccable.” Regardless, there is clear sympathy for or understanding of the perspective of Cain, a very unique position to take.

A Draco is a slang term used to describe a fully or semi-automatic firearm, such as an AK-47u/ a Mini AK-47.



However, due to the Firearms (Danger Air Weapons) Rules 1969, it is illegal for a member of the public to have a fully automatic rifle such as a “Draco.” As such, Future would likely have to smuggle his Draco into London if he wishes to “tote” it in London with “an extended” magazine.

It’s music that is going to be around forever. That’s the kind of music I make—astronaut music. People don’t understand what I’m saying. It’s big. It’s bigger than life.

It takes so long to get to Pluto. It’s not even a planet no more. So when you listen to this music, you got to think outside the box because it’s not going to be a time period. You are going to be listening to this album a year from now and you’ll just be catching up.

Tupac reflects on the psychological toll of his environment—PTSD, the pressure of survival, and the emotional push-pull of finding relief in weed while feeling guilt over it. Kendrick mirrors that same hypervigilant, combat-ready, shaped by trauma, so threats are serious.

His paranoia isn’t irrational—it’s strategic. and it mirrors Tupacs lyrics When Kendrick says:

meaning:
Grandmaster Melle Mel was the lead rapper and songwriter of Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five, the 1970’s New York hip-hop collective that not only pioneered the art of rapping, but the genre of hip-hop altogether.

https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/hip-hop-music/images/f/f0/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20140713083814 Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five, Grandmaster Melle Mel being the second man standing (left to right.)

To diss Melle Mel would be dissing rap and hip-hop itself, which Kendrick is well aware of and willing to do if necessary.

Lamar may be drawing parallels between his beef with Drake and J. Cole and the infamous 2023 beef between Grandmaster Melle Mel and hip-hop icon Eminem. The beef started back in a March 2023 Art of Dialogue interview where Mel suggested that Em’s #5 placement on Billboard’s top 50 Rappers of All Time list was solely because of racism:

Obviously, he’s a capable rapper. If you was talking about sales, he’s sold more than everybody. If you were talking about rhyme style, okay he got a rhyme style. But he’s white. He’s white! […] So now, if Eminem was another nigga like all the rest of us, would he be top five on that list when a nigga that could rhyme just as good as him is [ranked] 35? That had records and all that? He’s 35?

Em would go on to respond with a diss on “Realest,” a July 2023 track by Ez Mil where Em claimed Melle Mel lost his mind to steroid use:

Shout to the Furious Five and Grandmaster Flash but boy
There’s someone who really is furious, stay out his path, his wrath avoid
And I’ll be the last to toy with a juice head whose brain is like half-destroyed
Like a meteor hit it, well, there went Melle Mel, we lost his ass to ‘roids

Melle Mel replied with “Kickback,” an August 2023 diss track against Em that was so poorly received that Mel deleted the track from his YouTube channel and issued a public apology for both the song and starting the beef in the first place.

The last one is better
meaning:
Kendrick makes a callback to his 2012 song “Backseat Freestyle,” with lyrics from its chorus:

All my life I want money and power
respect my mind or die from lead shower

This line is a bold assertion where Kendrick claims superiority over Drake and J. Cole, the other rappers that form the so-called “big three” (from the hit song “First Person Shooter”) He uses part of his old rap name, “K. Dot,” to emphasize that he has the three most important things within the rap game: money, power, and respect.

This also is a nod to Deric “D-Dot” Angelettie, who produced The Lox' 1998 album Money, Power & Respect.

Special attention is drawn to respect, being, in Kendrick’s opinion, the best thing to have as a rapper. Kendrick has had a history of working on more conscious and less mainstream albums like To Pimp a Butterfly and Mr. Morale & The Big Steppers, with the five year wait for the latter album especially proving that he values quality and reputation over money.

“The last one is better” may also be a jab at Drake specifically — with him having a large amount of power and the most money out of the “big three” — but also lacking the respect given to Cole and Kendrick by many in the rap scheme.

Kendrick references hip-hop legend André 3000, who received attention online for being spotted carrying and playing a flute in various places around the world throughout 2023.



However, the “stick” Kendrick references isn’t a flute but a firearm. Considering the context of this being a rather direct diss, this is likely a direct shot at J. Cole. line: Ah, yeah, huh, yeah, get up with me Fuck sneak dissin’, first-person shooter, I hope they came with three switches
vault_lines: Ah, yeah, huh, yeah, get up with me
Fuck sneak dissin', first-person shooter, I hope they came with three switches
meaning:
Kendrick Lamar disses both Drake and J. Cole, directly replying to the latter’s line from their 2023 collab, “First Person Shooter,” off Drake’s For All The Dogs LP:

Love when they argue the hardest MC
Is it K-Dot? Is it Aubrey? Or me?
We the big three like we started a league, but right now, I feel like Muhammad Ali

The three are universally considered to be the greatest mainstream rappers of 2010’s hip-hop, i.e. “the big three” as dubbed by Cole. While Jermaine seemed to take a more friendly approach to the debate by collaborating with Drake, Kendrick rejects this civility altogether. In a sense, this is Kendrick standing firm on exactly what he said a little over a decade ago on 2013’s “Control” by Big Sean, where he famously declared:

I’m usually homeboys with the same niggas I’m rhymin' with
But this is hip-hop, and them niggas should know what time it is
And that goes for Jermaine Cole, […] Drake […]
I got love for you all, but I’m tryna murder you niggas

Kendrick lets both rappers know that their legacies will not outlive his, comparing his body of work to that of Prince, who outlived Michael Jackson by just under seven years. The two, while contemporaries of pop music for the better part of two decades, had a well-documented beef that spanned into the public sphere, just as Kendrick is now doing with his two fellow MCs. This also directly responds to Drake’s boast in “First Person Shooter” where he compares his commercial success to Michael Jackson’s:

What the fuck, bro? I’m one away from Michael
Nigga, beat it, nigga, beat it, what?

There are notable parallels between the two beefs, which Kendrick may very well be invoking: Kendrick and Prince have been generally acknowledged to have deeper artistic value in what they produce, albeit a step below their contemporaries in popularity, while Drake and Michael Jackson have been two of the biggest pop stars in each of their respective eras. On top of nearly collaborating with the late artist, Kendrick explicitly likens himself to Prince on the “Mask Off (Remix)” with Future (coincidentally) where Lamar says:

She said she broke down when Prince died (It’s alright)
Bitch, my hair down, Prince live through me (I am Prince)

Finally, Kendrick makes one last call out to the duo by calling them “dogs” that will end up being buried in the Pet Sematary, the title of a 1983 best-selling novel from horror writer Stephen King. It’s also a play on For All the Dogs, the aforementioned album that “First Person Shooter” is on. Making further wordplay, Dot compares his ammo to that of a “K” or an AK-47—a much more high-powered weapon than the “9” that Drake and Cole have, which is most likely a 9mm pistol—while also stringing the two guns together in the line to form “canine,” a term for dogs derived from their Latin name. “K” could alternatively be shorthand for Kendrick’s “K.Dot” moniker.

While Drake and Kendrick have been trading subtle shots at each other for years, it’s interesting that Lamar has brought Cole into this since the two have generally gotten along publicly. They even teased a collaborative album in Fall 2015 by rapping over each other’s beats on Black Friday.

It should also be noted how Kendrick chose to go after Drake on a song with Metro Boomin and Future, as the latter is a prolific collaborator with Drake. While it’s unknown if Future and Drake have active beef, Metro Boomin and Drake have been suspected to have disdain for each other in private.

Interestingly, Drake and Cole were on tour together promoting the former’s For All The Dogs on the It’s All A Blur Tour at the time of the song’s release.

Here, Future discusses his past life of poverty, danger, and distress: struggles and experiences which still affect him to this day. Further, nobody cared about him when he was living in poverty and did not have a name for himself. Once, he achieved success he gained influence, attention, and value. With his wealth, society could not ignore him any longer.

Future’s struggle reflect the unique experiences of a black man coming from poverty. As described by Crenshaw (1989), factors such as class, race, and gender all contribute to a unique multiplicity of hardship, a theory known as intersectionality. While people who are wealthy and white are assumed to have value in society the same is not true for black people, especially black men. Sadly, black men are required to prove their value to society by achieving substantial success, despite often facing more hardships in the form of systemic racism. This is the struggle Future outlines for us, as nobody cared to give Future notice until he achieved financial success.

line: [Intro]
meaning:
Future is interpolating the haunting theme song and calling card of Freddie Kruger, the main antagonist of the A Nightmare on Elm Street franchise. Freddie’s theme was created for the original 1984 film and has since reappeared in future installments, each time sung by a group of children jumping rope. Informally titled, “One, Two, Freddy’s Coming for You,” it’s a twist on the rhythm of the English nursery rhyme, “Buckle My Shoe,” albeit, the lyrics are swapped for ones that reference the dream-walking serial killer spirit:

One, two, Freddy’s coming for you
Three, four, better lock your door
Five, six, grab your crucifix
Seven, eight, gonna stay up late
Nine, ten, never sleep again

Future changes the lyrics again in his version to include subject matter more faithful to existing music across his discography, but without sacrificing the eeriness achieved by Wes Craven’s nursery rhyme. DMX famously flipped his own version of this refrain on his 1998 song, “X-Is Coming.”

It’s worth noting, Future actually featured on the remix to YNW Melly’s song titled “Freddy Krueger” in August 2021, a prior connection to the horror icon before he interpolated his theme.

line: Cross up the trap, I done broke down a key
vault_lines: Cross up the trap, I done broke down a key
meaning:
Cross up the trap": In basketball, to “cross up” means to use a dribbling move to confuse or outmaneuver a defender, effectively breaking down the defense’s structure to score. Applying this metaphorically to “the trap,” which stands for the environment of illegal drug trade, suggests Future is adept at navigating through the complexities and risks of this lifestyle. It implies a level of cunning and skill in overcoming obstacles and evading law enforcement or competition within the drug trade, akin to scoring against an opponent in basketball.

“I done broke down a key”: Breaking down a “key” (kilogram of drugs, typically cocaine) for sale is analogous to the detailed and strategic planning needed in both basketball to win games and in the drug trade to maximize profits. Just as breaking down a defense is crucial for scoring in basketball, breaking down a kilogram into smaller parts to sell reflects a successful strategy in the drug trade. This action indicates not just participation but proficiency and success, equating to “scoring” financially in the high-stakes world of drug trafficking.

line: Count up some millions then take some more drugs Been stuck in my memory, they wasn’t showing love
vault_lines: Count up some millions then take some more drugs
Been stuck in my memory, they wasn't showing love
meaning:
Count up some millions": This part of the lyric highlights the artist’s financial success. Counting millions signifies a vast amount of wealth, suggesting a level of achievement in the music industry or personal endeavors.

“then take some more drugs”: Following the mention of wealth, this line introduces the theme of substance use. In contrast to the success depicted by counting millions, taking drugs could be seen as a coping mechanism for dealing with underlying issues. It suggests that despite financial wealth, there are personal or psychological struggles that the artist is grappling with.

“Been stuck in my memory, they wasn’t showing love”: Here, the artist reflects on past experiences where he felt unloved or unsupported. “Stuck in my memory” indicates that these negative experiences have left a lasting impact, hinting at emotional or psychological scars. The lack of love and support might contribute to feelings of isolation or rejection.

line: I came out the jungle, they kidnapped a kid I trap out a bando, spent ten on a crib I look at the ocean to spot thirty M’s Pin it where I’m at, the city I’m in I give you my fully, no matter where I’m in
vault_lines: I came out the jungle, they kidnapped a kid
I trap out a bando, spent ten on a crib
I look at the ocean to spot thirty M's
Pin it where I'm at, the city I'm in
I give you my fully, no matter where I'm in
meaning:
“I came out the jungle, they kidnapped a kid”: This line metaphorically refers to coming from a tough, survival-oriented environment, often describing harsh urban realities. The “jungle” symbolizes a place of chaos and danger. “They kidnapped a kid” could suggest being forced into a lifestyle or situations beyond one’s control at a young age, possibly hinting at the challenges and adversities faced growing up.

“I trap out a bando, spent ten on a crib”: To “trap” refers to selling illegal substances out of a “bando,” slang for an abandoned house. This line contrasts his past life (trapping out of a bando) with his current success and wealth (spending ten million dollars on a house). It’s a reflection on his rise from poverty to affluence.

“I look at the ocean to spot thirty M’s”: Looking at the ocean likely symbolizes reflection and contemplation of his success, with “thirty M’s” referring to thirty million dollars. It implies he’s reached a level of success where he can literally see the vastness of his wealth and achievements, possibly comparing them to the expansive and endless ocean.

“Pin it where I’m at, the city I’m in”: This could be interpreted as marking his presence or impact on a place, suggesting that wherever he goes, he leaves a mark or is recognized. It might also imply a sense of pride in his roots or current location.

“I give you my fully, no matter where I’m in”: Offering his “fully” suggests giving his all or being completely committed, regardless of his circumstances or where he is. It reflects a theme of loyalty and dedication, possibly to his relationships, his crew, or his fans.

line: Lord, forgive me for my sins, I know this cash rules Everything around me
vault_lines: Lord, forgive me for my sins, I know this cash rules
meaning:
A reference to the legendary Wu-Tang song “C.R.E.A.M.”:

Cash rules everything around me C.R.E.A.M. get the money

Not only that, but Future splits the phrase between bars just as Biggie did when he made a C.R.E.A.M. reference. Ghostface himself did the same thing a short while afterwards.

Breaking the phrase up in this way proves convenient, as Future can kill two birds with one stone and make two points with one reference. Taking the phrase as intact, money holds so much power over the lives of the people around Future that he accidentally confuses it for what’s important, even though it’s actually the root of all evil. But taking the lines as they’re arranged, “everything around me” shifts from object to subject, and turns to “fast food”. And by fast food, Future means unfulfilling shit.

Driving backwards perfectly exemplifies this song’s message of making all the wrong choices in order to be with each other for one more night. Rather than moving on and driving away from each other (forward), they are driving right back to their broken relationship where they started from.

Angels are often used to represent a person’s good conscience. In cartoons or animation, they are often pictured on somebody’s shoulder (standing opposite of the devil) trying to convince them to make the right choice. Rihanna and Future are “dodging angels,” meaning that they are ignoring everything telling them to stop, even though they know it’s the right thing to do.

RiRi and Future could also be referring to guardian angels, in the sense that they are purposely avoiding something that is trying to save them from danger, or in this case, each other. Their common sense is being clouded by lust.



Broken lies and wrong words are synonymous. They are each saying what they know is wrong, just to be with each other. They both know what they’re saying isn’t really true; it’s just an excuse to be “selfish.”

This is reminiscent of Rihanna’s “Kiss It Better,” where she finds herself in the midst of a broken relationship, but rather than breaking up with him, she stays, simply because he makes her feel good.

meaning:
305 ‘was’ the area code for Miami and other surrounding areas in Florida, until it was overlaid by the 786 area code in the late 90s. However, by the time of the change, the 305 moniker had already solidified itself as a symbol for Miami culture. Many locals and rap culture in general have remained steadfast, still calling Miami “the 305.”

According to a feature in Billboard Magazine, Future himself owns a home in the 305, and he is quoted as saying of Miami that:

There’s a wide range of inspiration here.

In November 2017, Future threw his 34th birthday party in Miami at the at the lavish Versace Mansion (a.k.a. The Villa, Casa Casuarina).



The I-95 is a huge interstate highway that runs up the eastern coast of the United States from Miami, FL up through the border of Maine and Canada. It hits several major cities along the way, such as: Richmond, NYC, Philly, and Baltimore.

Driving 105mph on the I-95 near Miami would be considered well above the speed limit for Florida interstates, which have a maximum speed limit of 70mph.

meaning:
Pink Floyd was one of the most influential prog-rock bands of all time, with releases spanning from the mid-60’s to the mid-90’s.

Their most well known albums include The Dark Side of the Moon (1973), whose prismatic album artwork is one of the most iconic images in music history, and The Wall (1979), a double album widely recognized as a definitive example of both a concept album and rock opera.



Like HNDRXX album namesake Jimi Hendrix, much of Pink Floyd’s music draws upon psychedelia, to which Future compares lean’s influence on his own music. Further parallels can be drawn between Floyd and Future in their tumultuous creative and legal battles.

After founding member Syd Barrett, who was thought of as the creative force behind Pink Floyd in the early years, was officially removed from the band after just one album due to erratic behavior and speculation of mental illness, Roger Waters stepped forward as the front for the band during it’s most successful run from 1968 to 1985. He eventually left the band amidst creative differences. David Gilmour, who had replaced Barrett, became the leader of the band’s third incarnation despite legal disputes from Waters that argued against Gilmour’s rights to use the band name without him. Pink Floyd would continue to put out albums to commercial success, but with less critical praise.

Though Future’s singular creative prowess is unquestioned as a solo act, recent legal battles with former manager Rocko mirror the contractual obligations and disputes that spanned Pink Floyd’s tenure.

line: Cuban links on my bitch Cuban links on my bitch
vault_lines: Cuban links on my bitch
meaning:
A Cuban link is a type of necklace chain that is composed of interlocking links. These links are often flattened and tightly woven together, creating a dense, heavy chain that is both stylish and durable. The links themselves are usually wider than those found on other types of chains, giving the necklace a unique appearance.

Originally worn by wealthy Cuban families as a sign of their affluence and power, they found their way into hip-hop culture as a way for rappers to display their wealth and success – and ended up being a staple in the genre.

Choo’s name has been brought up multiple times in the rap industry, including in 2015 track “Jimmy Choo” from Fetty Wap, which mentions his shoes in the song numerous times.



The reason for adding this line to the song could connect back to the 2020 track “Jimmy Choo” from Karlae, featuring Gunna and specifically Young Thug, who is the main subject of this bonus song.

The follow-up “I feel fine now” signifies that Future feels better about himself after wearing the expensive shoes designed by Choo.

Future has also been a fan of Jimmy Choo for a long time, seen in ‘Made Myself a Boss’ and ‘Same Damn Time’. Pluto might also be signifying that one way he’s always coped with sadness and loss is by buying Jimmy Choo shoes.

Nicki compares the blue diamonds she’s worn to a party to the color of the American Democratic Party. Although Nicki has never exactly endorsed a political party, she’s spoken about things that tend to fall under Democratic party positions.

In 2012, for example, she gained attention from former democratic President Barack Obama for a diss of hers on republican Mitt Romney who was running for President against Obama at the time:

“I’m a Republican voting for Mitt Romney”
You lazy bitches is fucking up the economy

Furthermore, in 2016 she met with Obama to discuss a racial injustice initiative, and in 2018 she publically spoke against republican President Donald Trump’s “Zero Tolerance” immigration policy:

I came to this country as an illegal immigrant @ 5 years old. I can’t imagine the horror of being in a strange place & having my parents stripped away from me at the age of 5. This is so scary to me. Please stop this. Can you try to imagine the terror & panic these kids feel right now? Not knowing if their parents are dead or alive, if they’ll ever see them again…

Mexican cartel drug smugglers who bring cocaine over the U.S.-Mexican border tend to move at night so they don’t get spotted as easily.

When they took him in custody they took my life away

Esco’s stint in a foreign jail inspired his March 2015 mixtape 56 Nights.

line: Drink the dope and I get cool as a fan (Drink it up)
vault_lines: Drink the dope and I get cool as a fan (Drink it up)
meaning:
Here Future is saying, whenever he drinks his dope, he became cool as a fan.
“Dope” is a slang term for lean, purple drank etc (known by numerous local and street names) is a polysubstance drink used as a recreational drug. It is prepared by mixing prescription-grade cough or cold syrup containing an opioid drug and an anti-histamine drug with a soft drink and sometimes hard candy. The beverage originated in Houston as early as the 1960s and is popular in hip hop culture, especially within the Southern United States.[1] Codeine/promethazine syrup is usually used to make lean, but other syrups are also used.
 Because of the nature of the drug originally being a cough syrup, coupled with the cold soft drink it is mostly mixed with, it tends to produce a cold feeling whenever you drink or sip it like it is normally being done .

line: I got these regular hoes, I got superstar hoes takin’ pictures of me like the feds
vault_lines: I got these regular hoes, I got superstar hoes takin' pictures of me like the feds
meaning: Future contrasts “regular hoes” with “superstar hoes” to highlight the stark difference in the caliber of women he encounters. The term “regular hoes” likely refers to ordinary or average women, while “superstar hoes” suggests high-profile or glamorous women. Future’s use of the term “like the feds” adds another layer of meaning, implying that these women are documenting their interactions with him with the intensity of a federal investigation. This could suggest that his lifestyle and reputation attract attention and scrutiny, even from those in glamorous circles.

line: I put dope on my block, make the dope flip (Oh, woah)
vault_lines: I put dope on my block, make the dope flip (Oh, woah)
meaning: Future employs a clever wordplay using the term “dope” to refer to both narcotics and excellence. On one level, he suggests that he distributes drugs (“dope”) on his block to generate profit by selling them and making them “flip,” or turn a profit. However, there’s a double entendre at play here, as “dope” can also colloquially mean something impressive or excellent. So, in addition to the drug reference, Future may also be implying that he brings a high level of quality or excellence to his neighborhood or community, metaphorically “flipping” the perception of his surroundings. This line exemplifies Future’s skill in weaving together multiple meanings and layers of interpretation in his lyrics.

line: I’m big as a Beatle
meaning:
Future makes a reference to The Beatles, an English rock band comprising John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr. They are regarded as the most influential band of all time and were integral to the development of 1960s counterculture and the recognition of popular music as an art form.
More specifically, by early 1964, the Beatles were international stars and had achieved unprecedented levels of critical and commercial success. They became a leading force in Britain’s cultural resurgence, ushering in the British Invasion of the United States pop market.
